birth.stop: Rome, the house by the plane tree
birth.date_confidence: legendary. Trajan's reign (98-117) is attested history; the man Placidus is not. No second-century inscription, historian, or administrative record names him. The identification of this block as his house site is a Roman church tradition, first recorded centuries after the legend's own date, and the byname 'in platana' is the only thread holding it.

stops.stop: Rome, Trajan's Forum: the rank the legend gives him
stops.date_confidence: the reign is attested; the rank is an anachronism. The Latin tradition calls Placidus magister militum, an office created under Constantine in the fourth century and nonexistent under Trajan. The Greek Passio uses stratelates, which at least could have been spoken. Treat the Latin title as a later hagiographic gloss, not a Trajanic command.

Hadrian is in Syria at the accession and does not enter Rome until 9 July 118.

stops.stop: Saint-Denis, Suger's altar of Eustace
stops.date_confidence: attested by Suger (abbot 1122-1151), who records the first relics of Eustace in Europe at an altar of the royal basilica; the relic record is sometimes dated 1140. English Wikipedia adds the caveat that the Eustace venerated at Saint-Denis may have been Eustace of Luxeuil (d. 611).

stops.stop: Chartres, baie 43 in the nave aisle
stops.date_confidence: attested, with two corrections to an earlier draft of this dossier. The Chartres Eustace cycle is baie 43 in the nave aisle, glazed 1205-1215 (fr.wikipedia.org, 'Vitraux de la cathedrale de Chartres'), not the north transept rose: baie 121, the north rose, is c. 1230, dedicated to the Virgin, given by Louis IX and Blanche of Castile. stops.date_confidence: attested: Saint-Eustache, Quebec, founded 1770, incorporated 1835 (en.wikipedia.org, 'Saint-Eustache, Quebec'). Two corrections to an earlier draft of this dossier: the founding year is 1770, not 1780, and there is no Roman Catholic Diocese of Saint-Eustache. No such see exists; the town lies in the Diocese of Saint-Jerome-Mont-Laurier. The diocese claim is withdrawn.

stops.stop: Rome, four names come off the calendar
stops.date_confidence: attested: the 1969 revision of the General Roman Calendar (Calendarium Romanum, Consilium under Paul VI) removes the universal feasts of Barbara, Catherine of Alexandria, Christopher and Margaret of Antioch. Contradiction in the pool, recorded not resolved: one line of the research states that Eustace's own feast is removed in 1969 for the same reason, while the Fourteen Helpers file counts him among the ten left untouched. The atlas follows the arithmetic of the Fourteen file and flags the disagreement here.
